title: Hidden Ways We Lose Hours Every Week and How to Get Them Back ary-kelly/
author: Mary Kelly
summary: Leadership economist Mary Kelly argues that people rarely lack time; they unintentionally give away hours through hidden drains. She works through the main culprits, including interruptions that cost far more than their own length, meetings without a clear decision, reactive email, decision fatigue, busywork that disguises procrastination, multitasking, perfectionism, disorganization and saying yes too often. For each she offers a simple corrective, such as batching email, cancelling meetings with no decision to make and asking whether a task is important or merely comfortable. Her central leadership point is that the greatest time investment is developing other people, because coaching now saves many hours later. She concludes that successful people manage attention rather than time, repeatedly asking whether an activity is the highest and best use of the moment.
points: Research cited from UC Irvine suggests regaining full focus after an interruption can take more than 20 minutes.
Every meeting organizer should be able to name the decision the meeting exists to make, or cancel it.
Leaders preserve energy for important choices by reducing trivial decisions through routines, checklists and delegation.
Coaching employees feels slow but multiplies capacity, since leadership means building people who can do the work without you.
quotes: Everyone says they need more time, but time isn’t really the problem. Every one of us gets the same 24 hours each day. The difference is that some people unintentionally give away hours they never realize they’re losing.
Imagine being interrupted just six times during a workday. That’s not six lost minutes. It can easily become two hours of lost productivity, because one interruption rarely stays one interruption.
Every unnecessary meeting costs everyone in the room. The question every organizer should ask is simple: “What decision are we making?” If the answer isn’t clear, cancel the meeting.

Successful leaders reduce unnecessary decisions. They establish routines, automate recurring tasks, use checklists, and delegate whenever appropriate. In doing so, they preserve mental energy for the decisions that actually matter.
Every “yes” is also a “no.” When we say yes to one commitment, we are saying no to something else, and often that something else is family, health, strategic thinking, or rest.

Ironically, the best way to save time is to spend more of it developing other people. Many leaders hesitate to coach employees because it takes too long. Every hour spent teaching someone today may save dozens of hours later.
That’s why the most successful people don’t obsess over managing time. They manage attention.
